title: What is a living will?
intro: A living will, also called an advance directive or advance decision, is a written statement of the medical treatment you want or do not want if you can no longer make decisions yourself. It helps ensure your wishes are respected and relieves relatives of difficult decisions. Rules differ by country, so check local requirements.

sections.heading: Why have one
paragraphs: Illness or accident can leave a person unable to speak for themselves. A living will states in advance which treatments, such as resuscitation, ventilation, artificial feeding or dialysis, you would accept or refuse in specific situations. It guides doctors and family and shows your values.

sections.heading: What it contains
paragraphs: It should describe the situations it covers, for example severe brain damage, final stage of an incurable illness or advanced dementia, and name the treatments accepted or refused. It can include wishes about pain relief, place of care and organ donation, and your values. Specific wording is more useful than general statements.

sections.heading: Related documents
paragraphs: A healthcare power of attorney appoints a trusted person to decide for you and speak for your wishes. A care or treatment wishes statement is less formal. In some places, an emergency doctor's order is used for those with serious illness. Using several documents together creates a consistent picture.

sections.heading: Making and keeping it
paragraphs: Talk with your doctor, who can explain treatments and consequences, and with your family. Write it in your own words or use a template, sign and date it, and review it regularly, such as every few years or when your health changes. You can change or revoke it at any time. Give copies to your doctor, your representative and relatives, and note where it is kept.

sections.heading: Legal points
paragraphs: In many countries a properly written living will is binding. Requirements, such as written form or witnesses, differ, and some places allow it only in certain circumstances. A lawyer, notary, patient advice centre or doctor can help. It does not allow medical staff to end life actively.

examples.title: Starting the conversation
examples.text: Imagine you want to put your wishes in writing. You could discuss them with your family doctor and the person you trust most.

examples.title: Keeping it current
examples.text: Suppose your health changes. You might review your document, update it and give new copies to those who hold it.
